Notes: Earliest documented Jewish presence (basis for Year Established): limestone slab from Arsinoe-Krokodilopolis (capital of the Arsinoite nome; last seen in the antiquities trade at Medinet el-Fayum) recording that 'the Judaeans of Krokodilopolis dedicated this prayer house' (proseuche) for the well-being of King Ptolemy son of Ptolemy and Queen Berenike (Ptolemy III Euergetes and Berenike II). Dated c. 245-222 BCE; year = midpoint (c. -234). Refs: IEgJud (JIGRE) 117 = CPJ III 1532A = SB V 8939 = GRA III 186; trans. Kloppenborg. An organized community owning a prayer house; no count. Context (not counted): Encyclopaedia Judaica (Jewish Virtual Library) says the number of Jews settling in the Arsinoite nome (Fayum) grew under Ptolemy III - a nome-wide statement, not the capital. Jews in Fayum villages (Samareia, Trikomia, Alexandrou Nesos, Philadelphia etc.) are separate places and not counted here.

Loan agreement drawn up 'in Krokodilopolis in the Arsinoites district (nome)' dated 4 November 182 BCE: 'Apollonios son of Protogenes, Judean of the descent, has loaned to Sostratos son of Neoptolemos, Judean of the descent' (PTebt III 817 = CPJ I 23 = SB I 4232; TM 5396). Two named Judeans of military-settler descent active in the nome capital; presence only, no count.

Land-survey papyrus from Tebtunis (cited by the page as CPJ I 134, Tcherikover 1957) describing plots at Crocodilopolis-Arsinoe; its neighbours include 'a Jewish prayer hall [proseuche] represented by Pertollos, and a sacred garden cultivated by a tenant' and 'to the south the Jewish prayer hall [proseuche]'. The page dates it c. 113 BCE (CPJ: late 2nd c. BCE). Shows a Jewish prayer house owning land in the capital; no count. Encyclopaedia Judaica (Jewish Virtual Library, Egypt) likewise lists synagogues at Crocodilopolis-Arsinoe in the 3rd c. BCE, 2nd c. BCE and 2nd c. CE. Source is a popular website reproducing the CPJ translation; not checked against the scholarly edition.

Papyrus from Arsinoe 'dated just to the end of the first Jewish revolt' (CPJ II 421, Tcherikover-Fuks 1960, pp. 204-8) that 'lists the persons liable for the Jewish tax' instituted by Vespasian after 70 CE; 'All Jewish persons over the age of three were liable'; described as giving 'important and interesting demographic data'. The British Library catalogue (P.Lond. inv. 260/261) dates the register c. 73 CE and assigns it to Heraclides, amphodarch of the quarter of Apollonios' Camp (Apolloniou Parembole) in Arsinoe; its column summary of 173 names counts all adult males of that quarter, not Jews, so it is not used. A resident Jewish community in at least one city quarter just after 70 CE. Population blank: the register covers one quarter only and its count of Jews could not be accessed. Later (outside period): CPJ II 432 (113 CE), a water-supply account from Arsinoe, names a proseuche of the Theban Jews and a eucheion.
